turns.doctor_question: Hello, and welcome. I'm Dr. [Name], a psychiatrist. Thank you for coming in today. What brings you to see me?
turns.patient_response:
Well, doctor, I didn't exactly make the appointment myself. They... they sent me here. My lieutenant, actually, down at the station. It all happened in the bay, you know, where we keep the rigs parked and stocked, where everything is supposed to be ready to go. I was just... I was looking at the equipment, specifically the airway bags, and I realized they weren't right. They were all wrong. 

So I started moving them. I kept moving the airway bags into this specific pattern on the shelves because I just *knew* it was right, it was the only way they could sit to make sense. And while I was shifting them around, I was repeating the dispatch numbers out loud. Just saying them over and over, because the numbers and the physical bags, they have to align perfectly. It's a very specific sequence, you see? 

But then my lieutenant came over and he started getting loud, telling me to stop, telling me to step away from the equipment and take a breather. But I wouldn't. I couldn't step away. I told him no, because... well, because if I stopped, if I broke that sequence right then, it felt like the whole bay would go bad. The whole garage, the rigs, the concrete, everything would just go completely bad if I didn't finish the pattern. It was this intense, heavy pressure in the air, and I had to hold it together. So I kept doing it, I kept chanting the numbers, and he just wouldn't listen to why it was so important to finish. And... well, he pulled me off shift. Now they're making me talk to you before they'll even let me back on the trucks.

symptom_reasoning.S022: The patient describes engaging in bizarre, inappropriate behavior at work, including chanting numbers, rearranging equipment, and refusing to follow a superior's orders.
symptom_reasoning.S066: The patient describes performing repetitive behaviors (arranging bags in a specific pattern and chanting numbers) to prevent a dreaded, unrealistic outcome (the bay going 'bad').

turns.doctor_question: When you were arranging those airway bags and repeating the numbers, did part of you recognize that this might not be necessary, or did it feel completely real and necessary to you?
turns.patient_response:
Necessary? I... I don't think you're understanding the gravity of what was happening in that room. Of course it was necessary. It was the most real thing in the entire world. 

You see, when you're working the rigs, everything has a place, but it's more than just basic organization. It's... it's the alignment of it all. When I had my hands on those airway bags—the heavy canvas ones, you know, the ones with the O2 tanks and the intubation rolls packed inside—I could feel the exact weight of the dispatch numbers in my hands. Like, the numbers we get over the radio, they aren't just sounds that disappear. They correspond to the physical space in the bay. They anchor things. 

So when I was moving them, the air in the garage... it was getting so incredibly thick. You know how it feels right before a massive thunderstorm rolls in? When the barometric pressure drops so fast that your ears kind of pop, and the hair on your arms stands up, and you can barely pull a full breath because the atmosphere is just so heavy and charged? It was exactly like that. The concrete floor under my work boots was practically humming with it. I didn't have a single doubt in my mind. Not a fraction of one. 

Because if I put the pediatric bag on the wrong shelf, or if I stopped chanting the sequence—like, if I just stopped on a 10-52 instead of finishing the loop to close it out—that heavy, bad energy was going to seep right into the axles of the trucks. It was going to infect the oxygen lines. It was going to ruin the whole fleet and everyone who rode in them. I was the only one holding it together. So, no, part of me didn't think it was a mistake or unnecessary. I was actually... I was saving the shift. I was keeping the garage from going completely bad, and the lieutenant just couldn't feel the pressure in the room like I could. He just saw me moving canvas bags around, but he didn't see the actual structure of what was holding the room together. He just didn't get it.

symptom_reasoning.S019: The patient expresses a fixed, bizarre belief that their actions were literally preventing 'bad energy' from infecting the ambulance fleet, demonstrating a complete lack of insight.
symptom_reasoning.S066: The patient describes performing repetitive physical and mental acts (arranging bags, chanting sequences) to prevent an unrealistic, dreaded consequence (ruining the fleet).

turns.doctor_question: If I told you that dispatch numbers are just sounds and don't actually have physical weight or energy that could affect the trucks, would that make sense to you, or does that idea still feel completely wrong to you?
turns.patient_response:
I... I mean, I hear the words you're saying. "Just sounds." But I don't... I'm not sure how to even process that. I really don't know what you mean. 

Because when you're down there, when you've been working the trucks as long as I have, you know that sounds aren't just empty air. When the tones drop at 3 AM, and the dispatcher's voice comes crackling over the Motorola radio, it’s not just a noise that floats away. It hits your chest. It wakes you up out of a dead sleep and your heart rate instantly spikes to 130 beats a minute. You can literally feel the adrenaline dump into your bloodstream, making your hands shake while you pull your boots on. That’s a physical reaction, right? The sound changes the physical reality of my body. And then the diesel engines turn over, and the heavy exhaust fills the bay, and the whole concrete floor starts vibrating. 

So when you ask if it makes sense that they are just sounds without any weight... I don't know. I'm really not sure. Because in my experience, down in the garage, nothing is just a sound. The tones mean someone is trapped in a rolled-over vehicle out on the interstate, or someone is having a massive coronary, or a kid is choking. The sound carries all the weight of that reality. It brings it right into the room with us. 

When I was moving the airway bags—making sure the pediatric bag was exactly where it needed to be, making sure the trauma rolls were aligned—the numbers felt heavy because they *are* heavy. I don't know if that means your idea is completely wrong, or if I'm just not explaining the physics of it right to you. I'm an EMT, I have an associate's degree, I'm not a physicist or a scientist. I just know what I felt in my hands and what I felt in the air pressure of that room. I don't really understand how you can separate the sound of a dispatch from the physical reality of the rigs and the equipment. They're tied together. They have to be. So... I don't know. I honestly don't know if what you're saying makes sense. It just confuses me to try and strip all the weight away from the numbers like that, because that's just not how it works in the bay.

symptom_reasoning.S019: The patient maintains their fixed belief that dispatch numbers have physical weight and energy, rejecting the doctor's contradictory explanation that they are just sounds.

turns.doctor_question: When you were arranging those bags and feeling the pressure in the air, did any part of you think 'this doesn't make sense, I shouldn't be doing this, but I can't stop'—or did it feel like something you absolutely needed to do because it was the right thing?
turns.patient_response:
Like I was trying to explain earlier, doctor... it wasn't some kind of mistake in my head. I didn't have a little voice in the back of my mind saying, 'Oh, this is crazy, you shouldn't be doing this.' Not at all. It was absolutely, one hundred percent the right thing to do. The *only* thing to do. 

I mean, look, the whole reason they sent me here, the whole reason I'm sitting in this chair in your office right now, is exactly because of that. Because down at the station, I kept moving those airway bags—the heavy green ones, the blue pediatric ones—into that specific pattern that I just *knew* was right. I was moving them and repeating the dispatch numbers out loud, just chanting them into the air, over and over. And when my lieutenant came over and started getting loud, telling me to stop and step away... I wouldn't do it. I couldn't. 

You asked if I thought it didn't make sense? It made all the sense in the world. Imagine you're holding up a collapsing roof, right? And someone walks into the room and says, 'Hey, put your arms down, take a break, step away.' You wouldn't do it! You'd look at them and say, 'Are you blind? If I drop my arms, the whole building comes down on us!' That's exactly what it was like. The sequence of the bags and the numbers, it was the structural support for the entire garage at that moment. 

So when he was telling me to step away... I had to tell him no. I had to keep going. Because I knew, with absolute certainty, that if I broke that sequence, if I stopped chanting those numbers before the pattern was closed, the whole bay would just go completely bad. The rigs, the concrete, the oxygen lines, the whole fleet would just sour and go bad. I was protecting us. So, no, I didn't doubt it for a second. It wasn't some weird habit I couldn't stop. It was a necessity. I was doing exactly what had to be done, even if he couldn't see it.

turns.doctor_question: If your lieutenant or another firefighter you trust completely told you that they watched the bags all night and nothing bad happened to the trucks after you stopped arranging them, would that change how you think about what you experienced that day?
turns.patient_response:
Trust completely? I... look, doc, it’s not that simple. It really isn't. Because in EMS, trust is... well, it used to be everything. You’re in the back of a rig going 70 miles an hour down the interstate, you're trying to push meds or hold C-spine, and you have to trust the guy in the driver's seat with your life. But things at the station... things have shifted lately. The whole environment there has gotten so contaminated. So, if my lieutenant came up to me and said he watched the bags and nothing happened, I’d have to really wonder why he was saying it. I’d have to look at all the angles. 

Because I know for an absolute fact—and this isn't just a feeling, this is something I have tracked, something I see happening every single shift—I know the injury review people and some of the shift supervisors have been watching me. They use the station cameras. The ones mounted up in the corners of the bay, the ones by the supply closet, even the dome camera pointing at the dayroom door. They sit up there in the offices and they just watch me on the feeds. And it goes way beyond just keeping an eye on the floor to make sure chores are done. They have been going into the dispatch computer system, into my actual electronic patient care reports, and they are changing my triage notes. My actual, legal medical documentation! 

I'll type up a completely solid, by-the-book trauma assessment, I'll log the exact GCS score and the exact times, and the next day, the phrasing is different. The vitals are tweaked just enough. They are deliberately altering my documentation to make me look unsafe on the job. And when I try to bring it up, when I go to the office and say, 'Hey, why is my narrative changed?' or 'Why does this say I missed a step in the primary survey?' they just brush it off. They look me right in the eye, real calm, and tell me it’s just routine paperwork. 'Oh, it's just a QA audit, it's just routine.' Routine! It's not routine to sabotage a medic's license! They are building a whole fake paper trail to make me look incompetent. 

So, you ask if I'd believe the lieutenant if he said the trucks were fine? How could I? If the supervisors and the review board are watching me on the cameras and changing my triage notes to build this massive case against me, to make me look dangerous and unsafe, then anyone telling me 'the bags don't matter' is probably just trying to get me to drop my guard. They want me to stop arranging the bags so the fleet actually *does* go bad, and then they can blame the whole thing on me. They can point to their altered paperwork and say, 'See? We told you he was a liability.' So no, I wouldn't believe them. I can't. The whole chain of command is compromised right now. I have to trust my own hands and my own eyes, because they're the only things not lying to me.

symptom_reasoning.S019: The patient demonstrates a fixed, persecutory belief that supervisors are watching them via cameras and altering their medical documentation to sabotage their career, and explicitly states they would not change this belief even if a trusted colleague provided contradictory evidence.
symptom_reasoning.S066: The patient describes a need to continue 'arranging the bags' to prevent the fleet from 'going bad,' indicating a repetitive behavior performed to prevent a dreaded event that is not realistically connected.

turns.patient_response:
I mean... no, it wasn't always like this. If you're asking if this is some lifelong thing, absolutely not. I’ve been on the job, doing good, solid work for years without any of this happening. I was a respected EMT. But... let me think about the exact timeline, because it's important to get this straight, especially with how they're twisting things and building this file on me. It really started... yeah, it’s been about two months. About the last two months is when the whole environment completely shifted.

I remember it clearly because I was coming off a brutal 24-hour shift, we had just run this really messy MVC—a motor vehicle collision out on the county line—and I sat down in the dayroom to type up my charts. I was exhausted, just trying to get my narratives done so I could clock out. And I just happened to look up, and that dome camera, the one that’s been pointing at the vending machines since I started working there? It was physically rotated. It was angled right at my monitor. Right at the back of my head. That was exactly two months ago. And then, almost immediately after that, within days, that's when I started noticing the discrepancies in my electronic patient care reports. The little tweaks to my triage notes, the altered vitals I told you about. 

So, this whole situation—the camera surveillance, the paperwork being sabotaged, and then, you know, the stuff in the bay with the airway bags, all that station behavior that got the lieutenant and everyone so incredibly alarmed and got me sent to this office—all of that has been going on for about the last two months. Before that, nothing. Before that, everything was fine and I trusted the system. I trusted my supervisors. But these last eight weeks or so... it's just been a constant, everyday thing. Every single shift I walk in, I have to check the camera angles, I have to print out hard copies of my logs from the day before to prove they were changed, and I have to make sure the bags are right so the fleet doesn't go bad while they're busy trying to ruin my license. It’s been two solid months of just... having to be the only one who sees what's actually happening.
